notes.title: Ahaz in Assyrian records
notes.text: An inscription of Tiglath-pileser III lists "Jehoahaz (Ia-u-ha-zi) of Judah" among the kings who paid him tribute, about 734 BC. It is the same king, under the longer form of his name.

notes.title: Ahaz's age
notes.text: If Ahaz was twenty at his accession and reigned sixteen years, he died at thirty-six, yet 2 Kings 18:2 says his son Hezekiah was twenty-five when he began to reign, so Ahaz would have been about eleven at Hezekiah's birth. Some ancient witnesses (for example some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac) read "twenty-five". This is a well-known chronology puzzle.

notes.title: Burning children
notes.text: Cremated infant remains in urns, buried at sacred precincts called tophets, are well attested at Phoenician and Punic sites such as Carthage. Scholars debate how far these were sacrifices. The Bible says plainly that Judah's kings burned their sons (2 Kings 17:17; 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31). No tophet has been firmly identified in Judah.

notes.title: Shrines of the Judean kingdom
notes.text: Cult installations from the Judean monarchy have been found at Tel Arad and Tel Beersheba. At Beersheba a horned altar was found dismantled, its stones reused in a wall. Some link such finds to Hezekiah's reforms (2 Kings 18:4), though dating and interpretation are debated.
notes.source: Tel Arad and Tel Beersheba excavations

match: Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel
notes.title: Rezin and Pekah in Assyrian records
notes.text: Tiglath-pileser III names Rezin of Damascus (Ra-hi-a-nu) among his opponents. His inscriptions also say Israel's people "overthrew their king Pekah" and that he put Hoshea over them, matching 2 Kings 15:30.
notes.source: Tiglath-pileser III annals and Summary Inscriptions

notes.title: Edomites or Syrians
notes.text: The consonants of the Hebrew text give Aram (Syria); the traditional marginal reading (Qere) gives Edom. In Hebrew script the letters resh and dalet look alike. Because Elath lies on the Red Sea, far from Syria, many scholars prefer Edom, and KJV27 follows it.

notes.title: Elath
notes.text: Elath is the Red Sea port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. Tell el-Kheleifeh, long linked to Ezion-geber and Elath, has a fortress with Judean and Edomite phases, though its identification is debated.

match: I am your servant and your son
I am thy servant and thy son
notes.title: Vassal language
notes.text: "Servant" and "son" are standard Near Eastern vassal terms. In the Amarna letters (about 1350 BC), Canaanite rulers call the Egyptian king "my lord" and themselves his servants. Ahaz is placing himself under Assyria's authority, against Isaiah's advice (Isaiah 7:4-9).

match: carried its people into exile to Kir
carried [the people of] it captive to Kir
carried the people of it captive to Kir
notes.title: Amos 1:5
notes.text: Amos announced that "the people of Aram shall go into exile to Kir" (Amos 1:5), and Isaiah that Damascus would be plundered by the king of Assyria (Isaiah 8:4). Assyrian records confirm that Tiglath-pileser III conquered Damascus and deported people in 733-732 BC. The location of Kir is unknown.

notes.title: Isaiah's witness
notes.text: Isaiah 8:2 names "Uriah the priest" as a reliable witness for Isaiah's prophecy against Damascus and Samaria, in the same years. It is probably the same man.

notes.title: minchah
notes.text: Hebrew minchah is an offering of grain or flour, not of meat. The KJV "meat" meant food in 1611.

notes.title: The bronze Sea
notes.text: Solomon's huge bronze water basin rested on twelve bronze oxen (1 Kings 7:23-26). Mesopotamian temples also had large ritual water basins (the apsu). Ahaz removes it to pay or please Assyria. The Babylonians later broke it up (2 Kings 25:13).

notes.title: A rare word
notes.text: The Hebrew word (written musak, read mesak) occurs only here in the Bible. Its meaning is uncertain: translators guess a covered walkway, a throne canopy, or a Sabbath platform.

match: Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah
book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah
notes.title: Lost royal annals
notes.text: The writer of Kings repeatedly cites royal annals for Judah and Israel (1 Kings 14:19, 29). They are lost. Mesopotamian kings kept similar court chronicles, such as the Babylonian Chronicles that mention Judah's kings.

notes.title: Hezekiah's seal
notes.text: A clay seal impression found in Eilat Mazar's 2009 excavation on the Ophel in Jerusalem reads "Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz king of Judah". It is the first royal seal impression of a Judean king found in a controlled dig.
